pool.text: The whole of Portsea Island came united under the control of Portsmouth borough council.
Milton Road Cemetery was founded with approximately twenty-five acres of land.
A major terrorist incident occurred in the city leading to two deaths.
Portsmouth was bombed by a Zeppelin airship on the first day of October.
The Victory was placed in a permanent dry dock following a national appeal.
A memorial designed by Sir Robert Lorimer was unveiled by George VI.
Portsmouth gained its city status following a sustained campaign by the local borough council.
The city council incorporated the motto Heaven's Light Our Guide into the municipal coat of arms.
The Luftwaffe dropped 140 tonnes of high-explosive bombs during the heaviest raid on Portsmouth.
A V-1 flying bomb struck Newcomen Road, resulting in fifteen fatalities in Portsmouth.
The birthplace of Charles Dickens became a Grade I listed building.
The Soviet cruiser Ordzhonikidze arrived in Portsmouth harbour on a diplomatic mission.
The castle was withdrawn from active service and purchased by the city council.
Zurich Insurance Group relocated its United Kingdom headquarters to Portsmouth.
The remains of Henry VIII's flagship Mary Rose were rediscovered on the seabed.
The city formerly operated its own airport named Portsmouth Airport until its closure.
Portsmouth Central Library was built in the brutalist style in Guildhall Walk.
A British task force departed from Portsmouth to serve in the Falklands War.
Argentine forces launched an invasion of the Falkland Islands and South Georgia.
The Royal Marines Museum opened to the public under the National Heritage Act.
